title: How tinctures work
subtitle: A foundations reading on tincture preparation, ratios, and the solvent chemistry behind herbal extraction
excerpt: A tincture is a hydroethanolic extract of plant material, dried or fresh herb macerated in a mixture of water and alcohol. This reading explains the 1:5 and 1:3 ratios used throughout the herbal-medicine category, why alcohol percentage matters for different herbs, what cold maceration does and doesn't extract, and how to read tincture specifications. Covers standard strengths, dosing by ml, and the difference between fresh-plant and dried-plant tinctures.
sourceNotes: Original Homemade editorial. Method references: European Pharmacopoeia 9th edition, tinctures monograph; British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983), general methods; Hoffman D., Medical Herbalism (2003), solvent extraction principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of soaking plant material in a solvent (water-alcohol mixture) for 4 to 6 weeks to extract the soluble constituents. The plant material absorbs the solvent, cell walls soften, and the active compounds dissolve into the liquid over time. The longer the maceration, the more complete the extraction.

The solvent used in tincture-making, a mixture of ethanol (alcohol) and water in a specific proportion. The word comes from medieval alchemy, where 'menstruum' meant a dissolving fluid. The ratio of alcohol to water in the menstruum determines which plant constituents are extracted.

for 4 to 6 weeks. The alcohol preserves the extract, extends shelf life to two years or more, and acts as the primary solvent for resins, alkaloids, and many of the most therapeutically significant plant compounds. The water in the menstruum extracts the water-soluble active compounds, slippery compounds, tannins, glycosides. The ratio of alcohol to water is adjusted for the herb: high-resin herbs need a higher alcohol percentage. gel-rich herbs need more water.

Herbal extracts are described by a weight-to-volume (W:V) ratio, the amount of dried plant material (in grams) to solvent (in millilitres). A 1:5 herbal extract means 1 g of dried herb in 5 ml of menstruum. A 1:3 means 1 g in 3 ml, a stronger preparation with more plant material per millilitre. Most home herbal extracts for dried herbs use 1:5. fresh-plant herbal extracts often use 1:2 or 1:1 because the fresh herb contains water that dilutes the menstruum.

25% ABV: right for gel-rich and glycoside-rich herbs such as marshmallow, elderberry, and raspberry leaf. The low alcohol keeps water-based plant compounds intact without drying out gel-rich material.

40% ABV (standard vodka): the most versatile strength. Suitable for the majority of aerial-part and leaf herbal extracts, chamomile, lemon balm, thyme, motherwort, valerian. Standard plain 40% vodka is the home herbalist's default menstruum.
60% ABV: needed for resin-rich or hard-to-extract roots and bark, milk thistle seed, hawthorn berry, rosemary. At lower percentages, the resins remain in the plant material rather than dissolving.
Making 40% and 60% spirit without specialist suppliers

Standard supermarket vodka is 37 to 40% ABV, close enough to 40% for home herbal extract-making. For a 25% menstruum: mix equal volumes of 40% vodka and water. For a 60% menstruum: mix 3 parts 40% vodka with 1 part food-grade ethanol (available from homebrew suppliers), or purchase a 60% 'distilled grain spirit'.

Fresh-plant herbal extracts use a higher alcohol percentage (60 to 80%) to account for the water in the fresh herb. When fresh herb is covered in 40% spirit, the water from the plant dilutes the menstruum further, often resulting in a finished herbal extract below 25%, which may not adequately preserve it. The trade-off is that some volatile and enzymatic active compounds only survive fresh preparation. others are better concentrated in dried herb.

Standard dose for a 1:5 herbal extract of a dried herb: 2 to 5 ml, two to three times daily. A 5 ml dose delivers the equivalent of 1 g of dried herb. For a 1:3 preparation, the same dose delivers the equivalent of 1.7 g, roughly a third stronger. Doses are taken diluted in a small glass of water, not undiluted from the bottle.
What herbal extracts extract, and what they don't

Herbal extracts extract well: alkaloids, resins, bitters, aromatic oils, tannins, glycosides, flavonoids. They extract poorly: most large polysaccharides, starch, chlorophyll, and some minerals. For gel-rich herbs (marshmallow, slippery elm), a cold-water infusion extracts more than an herbal extract. This is why certain herbs are better prepared as herbal brews or infusions than as herbal extracts, the choice of preparation method matters as much as the choice of herb.
